q: A circular blue sign with a white arrow pointing up means:
options: You must turn left
You must go straight ahead only
Parking is allowed
No entry for vehicles
explanation: Blue circular signs with a white arrow show a mandatory direction; an upward arrow means traffic must proceed straight ahead only.

q: A blue circular sign showing a bicycle means:
options: Bicycles are prohibited
This lane is reserved for bicycles only
Cyclists must dismount
Bicycles have no right of way
explanation: A blue circle with a bicycle symbol is a mandatory sign marking a lane reserved exclusively for cyclists.

q: A triangular sign with a red border showing two children means:
options: A playground is ahead with no traffic
School or children crossing area ahead - drive carefully
Children are not allowed on this road
A pedestrian bridge is ahead
explanation: Red-bordered triangular signs warn of hazards ahead; the children symbol warns of a school zone or a place children may cross.

q: A triangular warning sign with a curved arrow indicates:
options: A U-turn is mandatory
A dangerous bend or curve ahead
A roundabout is ahead
Overtaking is allowed
explanation: This warning sign alerts drivers to slow down for a sharp bend or curve in the road ahead.

q: A blue rectangular sign with a white 'P' and a red diagonal line means:
options: Parking is available
Parking is not allowed here
Only police vehicles may park
Paid parking only
explanation: A 'P' with a red diagonal strike is an informatory/prohibitory sign meaning parking is not permitted in that area.

q: A green rectangular sign showing a hospital symbol tells drivers:
options: A hospital zone is ahead where they should reduce noise and speed
Only ambulances may use this road
There is no hospital nearby
U-turns are mandatory here
explanation: Green informatory signs guide drivers to facilities; a hospital symbol also signals a quiet, careful-driving zone nearby.

q: A green sign with a white arrow and 'Abu Dhabi' written on it is:
options: A warning sign
A directional/guide sign showing the route to Abu Dhabi
A mandatory sign
A speed limit sign
explanation: Green directional signs guide drivers toward cities, exits and destinations along the route.

q: A sign showing a white 'H' on a blue background indicates:
options: A helipad or hospital nearby
A highway entrance
A horse-crossing area
A holiday resort
explanation: The 'H' symbol on a blue informatory sign typically points drivers toward a hospital or helipad.

q: A red circle with a white horizontal bar means:
options: Give way ahead
No entry for all vehicles
One-way street
Speed limit ends
explanation: A plain red circle (no other symbol) is the standard 'No Entry' sign forbidding all vehicles from entering.

q: A triangular sign with an exclamation mark (!) generally warns of:
options: A general danger or hazard ahead not covered by a specific symbol
Road works finishing soon
A speed camera
End of a motorway
explanation: The exclamation mark is a general hazard warning used when no specific pictogram exists for the danger ahead.

q: At an uncontrolled intersection with no signs or signals, who has the right of way?
options: The vehicle on the right
The faster vehicle
The vehicle honking first
The larger vehicle
explanation: Where there is no signal or sign, the vehicle approaching from the right generally has priority in the UAE.

q: When an emergency vehicle approaches with sirens on, you should:
options: Speed up to clear the intersection first
Pull over safely to the side and let it pass
Stop immediately in your lane
Ignore it if you have the green light
explanation: Drivers must give way to emergency vehicles by pulling over safely, not by stopping abruptly in traffic.

q: Before changing lanes, a driver must:
options: Sound the horn only
Check mirrors, signal, and check blind spots
Flash headlights at other drivers
Change lanes quickly to avoid other traffic
explanation: Safe lane changes require checking mirrors, signalling in advance, and checking blind spots before moving.

q: Using a mobile phone (handheld) while driving in the UAE is:
options: Allowed if driving slowly
Allowed only at red lights
Prohibited and subject to a fine and black points
Allowed with one hand on the wheel
explanation: Handheld phone use while driving is illegal in the UAE and carries a fine plus black points on the licence.

q: When approaching a pedestrian crossing where people are waiting, a driver should:
options: Speed up to pass before they step out
Slow down and stop to let pedestrians cross safely
Honk to warn them not to cross
Only stop if a police officer is present
explanation: Drivers must give way to pedestrians at marked crossings by slowing down and stopping as needed.

q: Tailgating (following too closely) is dangerous mainly because:
options: It saves fuel
It reduces your reaction time if the vehicle ahead brakes suddenly
It is required on highways
It helps you overtake faster
explanation: Following too closely leaves no safe stopping distance if the vehicle ahead brakes suddenly, causing rear-end collisions.

q: At a junction controlled by a police officer whose signals conflict with traffic lights, a driver must:
options: Follow the traffic lights always
Follow the police officer's signals
Stop and wait for the lights to change
Choose whichever is safer for them
explanation: A police officer's hand signals always override traffic light signals at a junction.

q: Reversing on a highway or motorway is:
options: Allowed if there is no traffic
Strictly prohibited
Allowed only during the day
Allowed for trucks only
explanation: Reversing on a highway is extremely dangerous and strictly prohibited under UAE traffic law.

q: Unless otherwise signed, the general speed limit on Dubai's Sheikh Zayed Road is typically:
options: 80 km/h
100 km/h
120 km/h
160 km/h
explanation: Many sections of Sheikh Zayed Road are posted at 120 km/h, though this varies by section and is always governed by posted signs.

q: The default speed limit inside most residential areas in the UAE (unless posted otherwise) is around:
options: 40 km/h
60 km/h
80 km/h
100 km/h
explanation: Residential and internal roads commonly carry a lower posted limit, often around 40 km/h, to protect pedestrians.

q: A radar-tolerance margin means:
options: You can always drive that much faster than the limit legally
A small buffer above the posted limit before a fine is issued, which can change and should not be relied upon
There is no such thing in the UAE
It only applies to trucks
explanation: Radar tolerance is an operational buffer set by authorities and can change; drivers should always aim to obey the posted limit itself.

q: Driving significantly above the posted speed limit in the UAE can result in:
options: A verbal warning only
A fine, black points, and possible vehicle impoundment for extreme speeding
No penalty if no accident occurs
A discount on renewal fees
explanation: Excessive speeding is treated seriously, with escalating fines, black points, and impoundment for the most extreme cases.

q: Speed limit signs with a lower number displayed under the main limit on a variable sign usually indicate:
options: A permanent limit increase
A temporary reduced limit due to conditions like fog, rain, or roadworks
An error to be ignored
A limit for motorcycles only
explanation: Variable message speed signs lower the limit temporarily during poor visibility, bad weather, or road works for safety.

q: On a multi-lane highway, the leftmost (fast) lane is generally intended for:
options: Slow-moving vehicles
Overtaking only, not for continuous cruising
Parking in emergencies only
Trucks and buses
explanation: The leftmost lane on UAE highways is reserved for overtaking; drivers should return to the right after passing.

q: Black points on a UAE driving licence are used to:
options: Give discounts on registration
Track serious or repeated traffic violations and can lead to licence suspension
Reward safe drivers
Track fuel consumption
explanation: Black points accumulate for serious violations; reaching certain thresholds can suspend or revoke the driving licence.

q: If a driver accumulates 24 black points within one year, the usual consequence is:
options: A written warning only, with no other action
Licence confiscation for 3 months the first time, escalating to 6 then 12 months (plus a mandatory course) for repeat occurrences
An automatic fine only, with no action against the licence
Permanent, non-appealable licence cancellation on the first occurrence
explanation: Per the RTA Light Motor Vehicle Handbook, reaching 24 black points in a year leads to licence confiscation for three months the first time, six months if it happens again within a year, and twelve months (plus passing a special course) the third time.

q: Jumping a red traffic light in the UAE typically results in:
options: A verbal warning only
A fine of AED 800 and 8 black points
No fine, but 24 black points
A fine only, with no black points added
explanation: The RTA Light Motor Vehicle Handbook's violations table lists jumping a red light as an AED 800 fine carrying 8 black points.

q: Unpaid traffic fines in the UAE can result in:
options: No consequence beyond the amount owed
Vehicle registration renewal being blocked until fines are paid
Automatic cancellation of the fine after a year
A reduction in the fine amount over time
explanation: Outstanding fines must generally be cleared before vehicle registration (Mulkiya) can be renewed.

q: Driving without a valid licence in the UAE is:
options: A minor issue with no fine
A serious offence with a heavy fine and possible vehicle impoundment
Allowed for UAE residents only
Only an issue for tourists
explanation: Driving without a valid licence is a serious offence, carrying a substantial fine and the vehicle may be impounded.

q: Black points on a licence usually expire or are cleared:
options: Never
After a period of time set by the RTA if no further violations occur
Immediately after payment of the fine
Only when the licence is renewed
explanation: Black points typically clear after a defined period without further violations, according to RTA rules.

q: 'Lane discipline' on a highway mainly means:
options: Staying in one lane and only changing when necessary and safe, using signals
Switching lanes frequently to move faster
Always driving in the leftmost lane
Driving on the hard shoulder when busy
explanation: Good lane discipline means committing to a lane, signalling clearly, and changing only when necessary and safe.

q: The hard shoulder on a highway should be used for:
options: Overtaking during heavy traffic
Emergency stops only
A regular driving lane during rush hour
Parking to make a phone call
explanation: The hard shoulder is reserved strictly for emergencies, breakdowns, or use by emergency vehicles.

q: When merging onto a highway from an on-ramp, a driver should:
options: Stop at the end of the ramp and wait for a full gap
Match the highway's traffic speed and merge smoothly when safe
Force other vehicles to slow down
Merge only from the leftmost lane
explanation: Merging drivers should accelerate to match traffic speed and merge into a safe gap smoothly, without stopping unnecessarily.

q: Undertaking (overtaking from the right/inside lane) in the UAE is:
options: Always allowed on highways
Generally discouraged or prohibited and considered dangerous
Required when the left lane is occupied
Only for motorcycles
explanation: Undertaking is dangerous and against safe driving practice, since drivers do not expect to be passed from the inside.

q: A minimum safe following distance in good conditions is often measured using:
options: The 2-second rule (or more in poor conditions)
A fixed distance of 1 metre
No specific method is used
The width of the vehicle only
explanation: The 2-second rule (increased in rain, fog, or at higher speeds) helps drivers keep a safe following distance.

q: Sudden or unnecessary braking on a highway is dangerous because:
options: It saves fuel for the driver behind
It can cause multi-vehicle collisions from following traffic
It is required by law every few kilometres
It has no real risk on modern highways
explanation: Sudden braking without cause can trigger chain-reaction collisions, especially at highway speeds.

q: When entering a roundabout, a driver must generally give way to:
options: Traffic already circulating in the roundabout from the right
Traffic waiting to enter from other roads
No one, roundabouts have no priority rule
Only buses and trucks
explanation: Vehicles already inside the roundabout, approaching from the right, generally have priority over those entering.

q: To exit a roundabout, a driver should:
options: Never signal
Signal left before taking the exit
Signal right before taking the exit
Stop completely before exiting
explanation: Drivers should indicate left shortly before their exit to warn other road users and pedestrians of their intention.

q: At a signal-controlled intersection turning left with a green arrow, a driver:
options: Must yield to all oncoming traffic regardless of the arrow
May proceed with priority as protected traffic must wait
Should wait for a full green circle instead
Cannot turn left at all
explanation: A green arrow gives a protected turn; opposing traffic is normally held by a red signal during that phase.

q: At a four-way stop intersection with no signals, priority generally goes to:
options: The vehicle that arrived and stopped first
The vehicle turning left
The vehicle on the left
Whoever accelerates fastest
explanation: At an all-way stop, the vehicle that stops first generally proceeds first, with right-of-way rules applying for simultaneous arrivals.

q: When taking the first exit on a roundabout, a driver should generally approach in:
options: The leftmost lane and signal left on approach
The rightmost lane and signal left on approach
Any lane without signalling
The centre lane only
explanation: For the first exit, drivers typically stay in the right-hand lane and signal left as they approach the roundabout.

q: A yellow box junction (grid marking) on the road means:
options: You may stop there if traffic is heavy
Do not enter unless your exit is clear, to avoid blocking the junction
It is a designated parking area
It marks a pedestrian crossing only
explanation: Yellow box markings prevent drivers from entering and blocking an intersection when their exit route is not clear.

q: Parking in front of a fire hydrant or emergency access point is:
options: Allowed for a few minutes
Prohibited at all times
Allowed with hazard lights on
Only prohibited during working hours
explanation: Parking near fire hydrants or emergency access is prohibited at all times to keep access clear for emergency services.

q: Public parking spaces marked in yellow with a wheelchair symbol are reserved for:
options: Any vehicle during off-peak hours
Vehicles displaying a valid disability parking permit
Delivery vehicles only
VIP vehicles
explanation: These marked spaces are legally reserved for vehicles displaying a valid special-needs/disability permit.

q: Paid public parking in most UAE cities generally does not require payment during:
options: Public holidays and specific free hours as posted (e.g., certain evenings/Fridays)
Weekday mornings
Any time - parking is always free
School hours only
explanation: Many paid-parking zones waive charges on public holidays and certain posted free periods, but exact hours vary by emirate and zone.

q: Parking on a yellow-lined kerb generally means:
options: Free parking is allowed
Parking is restricted or prohibited
Parking is only for taxis
Loading zone with no restriction
explanation: Yellow kerb markings typically indicate restricted or prohibited parking, though exact rules are shown on nearby signs.

q: Double parking (parking beside an already parked vehicle, blocking a lane) is:
options: Allowed briefly for loading
Prohibited as it obstructs traffic
Only allowed at night
Allowed for taxis only
explanation: Double parking blocks the flow of traffic and is prohibited under UAE traffic regulations.

q: Under UAE Federal Traffic Law (Article 33 of the Executive By-Law), wearing a seatbelt is a legal requirement for:
options: The driver only
The driver and the front-seat passenger
Only children travelling in the vehicle
Only passengers when the vehicle exceeds 40 km/h
explanation: Article 33 of the Executive By-Law to UAE Federal Traffic Law No. 21 of 1995 legally requires the driver and the person seated next to the driver to wear a seatbelt. The RTA also strongly recommends every occupant buckle up, every trip, regardless of seat.

q: Children under a certain age/height in the UAE must generally travel:
options: On the front passenger's lap
In an appropriate child car seat in the rear seat
Standing in the rear seat
Anywhere, with no restriction
explanation: Young children must be secured in an age/size-appropriate child seat, and are generally not permitted in the front seat.

q: Not wearing a seatbelt while driving in the UAE can result in:
options: No penalty since it is only a recommendation
A fine and possibly black points
Only a warning for tourists
A penalty only if involved in an accident
explanation: Failing to wear a seatbelt is a ticketable offence carrying a fine, and in some cases black points.

q: Airbags combined with seatbelts work best because:
options: Airbags alone are always sufficient
The seatbelt keeps occupants properly positioned so the airbag can protect effectively
Airbags replace the need for a seatbelt
Seatbelts are only needed at high speed
explanation: Airbags are designed to work with a properly worn seatbelt; without it, occupants may not be correctly positioned for protection.

q: The legal blood alcohol limit for driving in the UAE is:
options: Same as many Western countries (a small allowed limit)
Zero tolerance - any detectable alcohol is illegal
Only enforced for professional drivers
explanation: Dubai enforces zero tolerance for drink driving: the RTA Light Motor Vehicle Handbook states that driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs is not permitted at all, with no allowance for any detectable amount.

q: Driving while fatigued is dangerous mainly because it:
options: Has no measurable effect on driving
Slows reaction time and can cause microsleeps, similar to impaired driving
Only affects long-distance truck drivers
Improves focus on monotonous roads
explanation: Fatigue slows reactions and can cause brief involuntary microsleeps, making it comparable in risk to alcohol impairment.

q: If you feel drowsy while driving on a long highway trip, you should:
options: Open the window and continue driving
Increase speed to reach the destination sooner
Stop at a safe place to rest before continuing
Drink more coffee and keep driving without stopping
explanation: The safest response to drowsiness is to stop in a safe location and rest, not to try to power through with stimulants alone.

q: Being caught driving under the influence of alcohol in the UAE typically results in:
options: A small fine only
Arrest, heavy fine, possible imprisonment, and licence suspension
A warning for first-time offenders
No consequence if no accident occurred
explanation: Driving under the influence is treated as a serious criminal offence in the UAE with severe legal consequences.

q: The vehicle registration card in the UAE is commonly known as:
options: Emirates ID
Mulkiya
Salik tag
Tawtheeq
explanation: 'Mulkiya' is the Arabic term commonly used for the vehicle registration card in the UAE.

q: Driving a vehicle with expired registration (Mulkiya) is:
options: Allowed for up to a week grace period with no issue
An offence that can result in a fine and the vehicle being impounded
Allowed if insurance is valid
Only a problem if stopped twice
explanation: Driving with an expired Mulkiya is an offence and can lead to a fine and vehicle impoundment.

q: Third-party liability insurance in the UAE is:
options: Optional for all vehicles
Mandatory for all registered vehicles
Only required for commercial vehicles
Only required for vehicles over 5 years old
explanation: Third-party liability insurance is a legal requirement for registering and operating any vehicle in the UAE.

q: 'Salik' in Dubai refers to:
options: A type of driving licence
An electronic toll collection system
A vehicle inspection centre
A traffic fine payment app
explanation: Salik is Dubai's automated toll-gate system that deducts a fee electronically as vehicles pass toll points.

q: A UAE vehicle must pass a periodic technical inspection mainly to:
options: Increase government revenue only
Ensure the vehicle meets safety and roadworthiness standards
Determine the resale value
Assign a new number plate every time
explanation: Periodic inspections check that a vehicle remains roadworthy and safe, covering brakes, lights, emissions, and tyres.

q: If involved in a minor accident with no injuries and both parties agree on fault, drivers in the UAE can typically:
options: Never move the vehicles and must always wait for police at any accident
Use a 'friendly' or minor-accident report process without necessarily waiting for police, depending on emirate procedure
Leave the scene immediately without any report
Only report the accident after a week
explanation: Many emirates allow a simplified minor-accident/'friendly' report process for small, no-injury collisions; procedures vary and drivers should confirm current local rules.

q: If you are fatigued while riding a motorcycle, you will:
options: Not be able to make decisions quickly
Be able to make decisions just as quickly as normal
Notice no difference in your riding
Ride more cautiously without even trying
explanation: Fatigue slows reaction time and judgement, making it harder to make quick, safe decisions while riding.

q: When checking a motorcycle's rear brake, it should be adjusted so that it:
options: Stops the motorcycle when only lightly applied
Stops the motorcycle when fully applied
Never fully stops the motorcycle
Locks immediately at any pressure
explanation: A correctly adjusted rear brake should bring the motorcycle to a stop when fully applied, without locking at the slightest touch.

q: When checking a motorcycle's front brake, it should be adjusted so that it:
options: Stops the motorcycle when only lightly applied
Stops the motorcycle when fully applied
Does not stop the motorcycle even when fully applied
Only works when the engine is off
explanation: Like the rear brake, a correctly adjusted front brake should stop the motorcycle when fully applied.

q: What should each mirror fitted to a motorcycle let the rider see?
options: Mainly the traffic directly behind
Only the lane next to the rider
As much as possible of the lane next to the rider and of the traffic behind
Nothing in front of the rider
explanation: Motorcycle mirrors should be adjusted to show as much as possible of the adjacent lane and the traffic behind, to cover blind spots.

q: Why is it dangerous to use a second-hand (used) motorcycle helmet?
options: It may have damage that is not visible from the outside
It may simply be an outdated design
It is not considered socially acceptable
It is always the wrong size
explanation: A used helmet may have suffered an impact that weakened its protective foam without leaving visible external damage, so its crash protection can no longer be trusted.

q: When fully applied, which brakes should be able to hold a stationary motorcycle?
options: The front brake only
The rear brake only
Both the front and rear brakes
Neither brake; only the side stand holds the bike
explanation: Both the front and rear brakes, when fully applied and in good working order, should each be capable of holding the motorcycle stationary.

q: When a motorcycle's throttle is opened wide and then released, it should:
options: Snap shut
Gradually close over several seconds
Remain in place until manually closed
Continue accelerating briefly
explanation: A healthy throttle return spring should snap the throttle fully shut as soon as it is released, which is an important pre-ride safety check.

q: A motorcycle's drive chain should:
options: Have no slack at all
Be lubricated and have its tension adjusted correctly
Always have 10-20 mm of slack no matter what the manual says
Never be checked once it is fitted
explanation: The chain should be kept lubricated with its tension set to the manufacturer's specification; too tight or too loose can cause premature wear or a dangerous failure.

q: When riding through a corner, a motorcycle rider should:
options: Stay right of centre in the lane to keep away from oncoming vehicles
Stay left of centre in the lane to be more easily seen
Position on the road so they can see through the corner and be seen by other drivers
Always ride in the exact centre of the lane regardless of visibility
explanation: Good cornering technique means positioning yourself in the lane for the best view through the bend and the best visibility to other road users, adjusting position as the corner requires.

q: Under UAE traffic law, wearing an approved helmet on a motorcycle is required for:
options: The rider only
The rider and any pillion (passenger)
Only riders under 18 years old
Only when riding on highways, not urban roads
explanation: Confirmed in the RTA-affiliated Drive Dubai motorcycle theory-test training deck: when riding with a pillion passenger, an approved helmet is required for both the rider and the pillion passenger, not the rider alone.

q: Lane splitting (riding a motorcycle between lanes of stationary or slow-moving traffic) in the UAE is:
options: Legal at any speed difference between the motorcycle and the traffic
Generally not permitted; motorcycles must keep to a marked lane like other vehicles
Only illegal on Sheikh Zayed Road
Actively encouraged by the RTA to reduce congestion
explanation: UAE practice generally treats lane splitting as not permitted, with motorcycles expected to stay within a marked lane, but this pass could not confirm the exact statutory article, so it remains flagged for verification against the current traffic law text.

q: When carrying a pillion passenger on a motorcycle in the UAE, the rider must ensure:
options: No more than one pillion passenger, seated on a proper seat with footrests and wearing a helmet
Up to two pillion passengers are allowed if the motorcycle is large enough
The pillion passenger does not need a helmet if the trip is short
There is no restriction on the number of passengers carried
explanation: Standard motorcycle safety practice limits a motorcycle to one pillion passenger, properly seated and helmeted; the exact UAE statutory limit was not directly confirmed in the sources used for this pass, so it remains flagged.

q: For heavy vehicle and bus drivers, the best time to take a rest break is:
options: Before you become tired
As soon as you become tired
Only once you reach your final destination
Only during specific RTA-designated hours
explanation: Planning rest breaks before fatigue sets in, rather than waiting until you already feel tired, is the recommended approach in heavy-vehicle driver training.

q: Which of the following is most likely to cause drowsiness while driving a heavy vehicle?
options: Taking cold and allergy tablets
Suffering from mild hay fever
Taking a short nap before starting to drive
Opening a window for fresh air
explanation: Many cold and allergy (antihistamine) medications cause drowsiness as a side effect, which is a serious risk for a driver; a short nap before driving actually helps alertness.

q: Which food choice is best for a heavy vehicle driver during a long trip?
options: A heavy, fried meal
A bag of fresh fruit
A large bowl of pasta
Sugary snacks and energy drinks only
explanation: Light, fresh food such as fruit is easier to digest and less likely to cause the sluggishness that heavy or sugary meals can bring on during a long drive.

q: The best way to help prevent fatigue on a long-distance trip is to travel during:
options: The hours you are normally awake
Daylight hours only, regardless of your normal sleep pattern
Night hours only, to avoid traffic
It makes no difference when you travel
explanation: Driving during your normal waking hours works with your body clock, while driving through your usual sleep hours increases the risk of fatigue regardless of whether it is day or night.

q: During a rest stop on a long trip, light exercise such as stretching or touching your toes:
options: Can help keep you alert
Has no effect on alertness
Should never be done before a long trip
Increases fatigue
explanation: Light physical activity during a break helps circulation and alertness, making it a useful part of managing fatigue on long trips.

q: Rocks or mud caught in the space between a heavy vehicle's dual (twin) wheels may cause:
options: A tyre to lose pressure
The engine to overheat
The gearbox to slip
No effect on the tyres at all
explanation: The Truck and Bus Handbook's pre-trip inspection checklist states: rocks or mud caught between dual wheels can unbalance a wheel and damage the tyre side walls and wheel bearings — which is why drivers must check the spacing between dual wheels.

q: Under RTA rules, a heavy vehicle failing to keep proper lane discipline (using lanes not permitted for heavy vehicles) is a violation that carries:
options: A fine of AED 600 and 6 black points
A fine of AED 5000 and no black points
No fine, only a verbal warning
Automatic and immediate licence cancellation
explanation: The RTA Light Motor Vehicle Handbook's violations table lists heavy-vehicle lane discipline breaches with a fine of AED 600 and 6 black points.

q: Overloading a heavy vehicle, or having its load protrude without permission, is a violation that carries:
options: A fine of AED 500 and 6 black points
No fine, only vehicle impoundment
A fine of AED 5000 and 12 black points
A warning only, for the first offence
explanation: The RTA handbook's violations table lists overloading or an unauthorised protruding load from a heavy vehicle with a fine of AED 500 and 6 black points.

q: A load that falls or leaks from a heavy vehicle onto the road is a violation that carries:
options: A fine of AED 3000 and 21 black points
A fine of AED 100 and no black points
No fine if the load is retrieved quickly
A fine, but no black points at all
explanation: The RTA handbook's violations table lists a falling or leaking load with a fine of AED 3000 and 21 black points -- one of the more serious violations short of court-decided offences.

q: Dangerous overtaking by a truck is a violation under RTA rules that carries:
options: A fine of AED 800 and 24 black points
A fine of AED 200 and 2 black points
No black points, a fine only
A warning only, no fine
explanation: The RTA handbook's violations table lists dangerous overtaking by trucks with a fine of AED 800 and 24 black points -- the same severe points tier as driving without number plates.

q: Failing to cover the load of a truck (for example, loose gravel or sand) in the UAE carries:
options: A fine of AED 3000
No fine, a verbal warning only
A fine of AED 50
Suspension of the vehicle's registration only, with no fine
explanation: The RTA handbook's violations table lists not covering a truck's load with a fine of AED 3000.

q: According to the RTA's Truck and Bus Handbook, a heavy vehicle or bus driver should never drive for more than how many hours within any 24-hour period?
options: 6 hours
8 hours
10 hours
12 hours
explanation: Verified in the RTA Truck and Bus Handbook (Part 2, 'Take Breaks'): drivers should take short breaks before becoming tired and should never drive for more than 10 hours in any 24-hour period.

q: The red octagonal sign with a white border reading "STOP" means:
options: Slow down and proceed if the road looks clear
You must come to a complete stop before proceeding, even if the road looks clear
Give way only to traffic coming from your right
Sound your horn before moving off
explanation: The eight-sided red STOP sign requires every driver to come to a full stop at the marked line or before the intersection, then proceed only when it is safe.

q: A red circular sign with a solid white horizontal bar and no other markings means:
options: No entry for any vehicle from this direction
One-way street ahead
No parking allowed here
The speed limit shown earlier now ends
explanation: This is the international 'No Entry' sign: vehicles must not enter the road from this direction, even though traffic or pedestrians on the other side may still use it.

q: A red-ringed circular sign showing a U-shaped arrow struck through with a red line means:
options: You must not overtake here
You must not make a U-turn at this point
You must not reverse here
You must not park facing either direction
explanation: This is the RTA handbook's 'No U-turn' prohibitory sign: drivers must not turn their vehicle around to face the opposite direction at that location.

q: A circular sign, ringed in red, showing a black car and a red car side by side means:
options: Overtaking is prohibited on this stretch of road
Two-way traffic begins ahead
A dual carriageway begins here
Slow-moving vehicles must keep to the left lane
explanation: This is the RTA handbook's 'You must not overtake' prohibitory sign. Overtaking is banned until the road ends the restriction or another sign cancels it.

q: In the UAE, the standard shape and colour scheme used for advance warning signs (curves, junctions, pedestrian crossings ahead, etc.) is:
options: A red-bordered triangle with a black symbol on a white background
A blue circle with a white symbol
A green rectangle with white text
A red octagon with white text
explanation: Advance warning signs follow the international convention of a red-bordered triangle with a black pictogram on white, giving drivers early notice of a hazard ahead.

q: Black-and-yellow chevron arrow signs mounted right at a sharp bend are used to:
options: Advertise a nearby exit or service station
Mark the exact direction and sharpness of the bend itself, as a hazard marker at the hazard
Show a mandatory direction of travel
Indicate the start of a freeway on-ramp
explanation: The RTA handbook classes these as hazard marker signs, distinct from the earlier triangular advance-warning sign for the same curve: they mark the physical hazard itself, right where it is.

q: The signs marking 'the beginning of a freeway' and 'the end of a freeway' are both classified in the RTA handbook as:
options: Freeway control signs
Warning signs
Parking control signs
Informatory signs only
explanation: Freeway control signs are one of the five categories of regulatory sign in the RTA handbook, used to show road users exactly where a freeway section starts and ends.

q: A warning sign showing a camel silhouette on the road most likely warns that:
options: You are entering a wildlife sanctuary
Domestic animals such as camels, sheep or goats may be herded across or wander onto the road
A camel-racing track is ahead
A livestock market exit is nearby
explanation: Per the RTA handbook, the camel symbol can also represent sheep or goats; slow down, leave animals plenty of space, and never sound your horn near them as it may startle them into the road.

q: A blue circular sign showing a white arrow curving to indicate travel direction around a roundabout is an example of a:
options: Warning sign
Parking control sign
Control sign, showing right-of-way priority or direction of travel
Freeway control sign
explanation: The RTA handbook groups roundabout-direction arrows under control signs, the category used to assign right-of-way priority or a required direction of travel.

q: A blue rectangular sign marked with a large white "P" indicates:
options: No parking allowed in this area
An area where parking is permitted, subject to any conditions shown on the sign
A police station ahead
A pedestrian-only zone
explanation: A blue sign with a white 'P' is a parking control sign showing where parking is permitted; a red circle with a diagonal line through a 'P' shows the opposite — parking prohibited.

q: When entering a roundabout in the UAE, you must give way to:
options: Vehicles already on the roundabout, approaching from your left
Vehicles already on the roundabout, approaching from your right
Only vehicles that are signalling to exit
No one, if you are already in the outer lane
explanation: Per the RTA handbook, once you have chosen your lane on approach, you must give way to all vehicles already circulating on the roundabout that are moving towards you from the left, entering only when it is safe.

q: A police or ambulance vehicle approaches from behind with its siren and flashing lights on, while you are stopped at a green light. You should:
options: Ignore it, since your light is green
Give way and move clear of its path as quickly and safely as possible, even though your light is green
Speed up to clear the intersection before it arrives
Give way only if it is a police car, not an ambulance
explanation: The RTA handbook states that emergency vehicles have priority whenever their siren is on or they show flashing lights; drivers must give way and stop if necessary despite any other rule, including having a green light.

q: A school bus ahead has stopped with its electronic stop arm extended and its lights flashing. You should:
options: Overtake carefully at reduced speed
Sound your horn to alert the children, then pass
Not pass the bus while the stop arm is extended and its flashers are working; slow down and be ready to stop
Only stop once you can see a child actually crossing
explanation: The RTA handbook instructs drivers to be patient and avoid passing a stopped school bus while its stop arm and flashers are active, since children nearby can be unpredictable and may cross suddenly.

q: At a marked pedestrian crossing where people are already crossing, a driver must:
options: Give way to the pedestrians and not proceed until the crossing is clear
Proceed slowly through the crossing
Sound the horn so the pedestrians hurry up
Only stop if a traffic signal also shows red
explanation: Not giving way to pedestrians on a pedestrian crossing is listed in the RTA handbook's traffic-violations table as a serious offence — drivers must always give way to pedestrians already using a crossing.

q: If a driver accumulates 24 black points within one year for the first time, the licence is:
options: Cancelled permanently
Confiscated for 3 months
Confiscated for 6 months
Confiscated for 12 months, with a mandatory course required
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: reaching 24 points in a year leads to a 3-month licence confiscation the first time, 6 months the second time it happens again within a year, and 12 months plus a mandatory special course the third time.

q: Driving in a dedicated bus or taxi lane in Dubai without authorisation carries a fine of:
options: AED 200
AED 400
AED 600
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: any driver caught illegally using a bus or taxi lane will be fined AED 600.

q: Passing a Salik toll point without a valid tag fitted to the vehicle results in a fine that:
options: Stays fixed at AED 50 no matter how many times it happens
Escalates: AED 100 for the first trip, AED 200 for the second, AED 400 for the third and every trip after that
Is only a warning, with no fine for the first three times
Is capped at AED 24, the same as the daily toll maximum
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook's Salik violations table: passing without a tag is fined AED 100 (first trip), AED 200 (second trip), and AED 400 (third and subsequent trips).

q: Each time a vehicle with a valid Salik tag passes a tolling point, the amount deducted and the daily maximum charge are:
options: AED 2 per toll, with no daily maximum
AED 4 per toll, with a maximum of AED 24 per day
AED 4 per toll, with a maximum of AED 40 per day
AED 10 per toll, with a maximum of AED 50 per day
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: AED 4.00 is deducted at each Salik tolling point, with a maximum total toll charge of AED 24.00 per day.

q: When overtaking a cyclist or motorcyclist, a driver should:
options: Pass as close as possible to save road space
Only move left if an entire lane is completely free first
Move safely to the left, leaving at least one metre of clearance
Sound the horn continuously while passing
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: drivers should only overtake a cyclist or motorcyclist if they can safely move left, leaving at least one metre of clearance, especially useful near parked cars where a door could open unexpectedly.

q: Motorcyclists and cyclists in the UAE are permitted to:
options: Use only the far-left edge of their lane at all times
Use the full width of their traffic lane
Ride two-abreast in the same lane as cars, without restriction
Use the hard shoulder as a dedicated riding lane
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: motorcyclists and cyclists are permitted to use the full width of the road lane, so other drivers must leave them enough space to do so safely.

q: On a UAE freeway, overtaking another vehicle by using the hard shoulder is:
options: Allowed if your vehicle is a truck
Allowed only during heavy congestion
Not allowed under any circumstance
Allowed if you signal clearly first
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: drivers must not overtake on the hard shoulder of the road; it is reserved for emergencies and breakdowns, not for bypassing traffic.

q: A heavy vehicle that causes a falling or leaking load on the road is penalised with:
options: 6 black points
12 black points
21 black points
24 black points
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook's violations table: a falling or leaking load carries 21 black points, reflecting the serious hazard it creates for following traffic.

q: Unless a sign states otherwise, the default speed limit on an urban single carriageway road in Dubai is:
options: 25 km/h
40 km/h
60 km/h
80 km/h
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook's speed limit table: urban single carriageway roads default to 40 km/h unless signed otherwise.

q: On an urban dual carriageway in Dubai, the default speed limit (unless signed otherwise) is:
options: 40 km/h
60 km/h or 80 km/h as signed
100 km/h
120 km/h
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: urban dual carriageways are set at 60 km/h or 80 km/h, as shown by the posted sign.

q: The default speed limit on rural roads in Dubai (unless a sign shows otherwise) is:
options: 60 km/h
80 km/h
100 km/h
120 km/h
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook's speed limit table: rural roads default to 100 km/h.

q: On Dubai freeways, the maximum speed limit is 120 km/h for light vehicles and, for heavy vehicles, it is:
options: 60 km/h
80 km/h
100 km/h
120 km/h
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: freeways allow up to 120 km/h for light vehicles but only 80 km/h for heavy vehicles.

q: On Dubai freeways, in addition to the maximum limit, there is also a minimum speed limit of:
options: 40 km/h
60 km/h
80 km/h
100 km/h
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: freeways carry a minimum speed limit of 60 km/h, alongside the maximum limits for light and heavy vehicles.

q: The speed limit inside a parking area or on a service road in Dubai is typically:
options: 15 km/h
25 km/h
40 km/h
60 km/h
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook's speed limit table: parking areas and service roads default to 25 km/h.

q: When overtaking another vehicle travelling in the same direction, you must pass on:
options: Either side, whichever is clearer
The left only
The right only
The hard shoulder
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook (Article 10.5): a driver must only pass other vehicles travelling in the same direction on the left.

q: If another vehicle is overtaking you, the correct response is to:
options: Speed up so it cannot pass
Slow down and keep to the right
Move to the left lane immediately
Flash your headlights and hold your lane
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook (Article 54): if someone is overtaking you, you must slow down and keep to the right.

q: According to the RTA handbook, you must NOT overtake at:
options: A straight, clear stretch of road
Intersections and roundabouts
A dual carriageway with a broken centre line
A designated overtaking lane
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: overtaking is prohibited where the road is not clearly visible, when oncoming traffic doesn't allow it safely, and specifically at intersections and roundabouts.

q: Before pulling out to overtake a vehicle on a two-way road, the handbook advises staying at least how far behind it?
options: Half a second
Two seconds
Ten seconds
One car length only
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: you should be at least two seconds behind the vehicle you are about to overtake, giving better vision and room to build up speed.

q: According to the RTA handbook, overtaking a large truck on the open road typically takes about:
options: 5 seconds
25 seconds
60 seconds
2 minutes
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: it takes about 25 seconds to overtake a large truck on the open road, which is a long time to spend on the wrong side of the road.

q: You must not cross which type of line to overtake another vehicle?
options: A single broken white line
A single solid white/yellow line dividing traffic
Lane arrows painted on the road
A pedestrian crossing's zebra markings
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook (Article 58): you must not cross a single solid line on the road which divides traffic, whether to overtake or to turn, except in an emergency.

q: When travelling around a roundabout in the UAE, you should keep to which side of the central island?
options: The left
The right
Either side, no rule applies
Straddle the centre line
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: at a roundabout you should always keep to the right of the central island, travelling around it in an anti-clockwise direction.

q: As you are about to enter a roundabout, you must give way to:
options: Vehicles behind you
Vehicles already in the roundabout approaching from your left
Vehicles waiting at other entrances
Pedestrians only
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: once you have selected the correct lane and are about to enter the roundabout, you must give way to all vehicles already in it moving towards you from the left.

q: On a two-lane roundabout, if you intend to turn right, you should:
options: Approach and stay in the left lane
Approach in the right lane and leave in the right-hand lane
Use either lane and switch freely
Enter from the hard shoulder
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: for a two-lane roundabout, turning right means approaching in the right lane, staying in it, signalling right, and leaving in the right-hand lane.

q: On a three-lane roundabout, which lane is reserved only for vehicles turning left?
options: The right-hand lane
The centre lane
The left-hand lane
Any lane may be used
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: on a three-lane roundabout you should not choose the left-hand lane unless turning left, as that lane is reserved for left-turning vehicles only.

q: At an intersection without signals, where a minor road meets a main road, priority must generally be given to:
options: Whichever vehicle arrives first
Vehicles coming from the main road
Vehicles turning left
The larger vehicle
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: at such intersections, priority of crossing must be given to vehicles coming from a main road; where there is a roundabout, priority goes to vehicles already in it.

q: According to the RTA handbook's 2010 crash data, what proportion of crashes in Dubai were caused by drivers under the influence of alcohol?
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: it states that 14.33% of crashes in Dubai are caused by drivers who were under the influence of alcohol.

q: Alcohol and drugs make driving dangerous mainly because they:
options: Improve your reaction time
Make it harder to judge risks, distance and speed, and give a false sense of confidence
Only affect your sense of smell
Have no effect on judgement, only on movement
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: alcohol and drugs make it more difficult to judge risks including distance and speed, and give a false sense of confidence that can encourage risk-taking.

q: If you have been drinking, the safest plan before driving is to:
options: Drink coffee and wait 10 minutes
Open the windows and drive slowly
Arrange to be picked up by someone alcohol-free, or take a taxi
Drive only on familiar roads
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: to stay safe, plan ahead and arrange to be picked up by someone who is alcohol or drug free, or take a taxi.

q: Rumble strips on the road are especially helpful for drivers who are:
options: Speeding
Tired or drowsy on a long drive
Reversing
Towing a trailer
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: rumble strips warn drivers approaching a hazard, and this vibration and sound is especially helpful for drivers on a long drive who may be feeling tired or sleepy.

q: A rear-facing infant car seat should never be placed:
options: In the back seat
On the front passenger seat with an active airbag
Behind the driver
In the middle rear seat
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: rear-facing car seats should never be placed on the front passenger seat, as a deploying airbag can cause fatal injuries to the infant.

q: According to the RTA handbook's safety guidance, children should generally ride in the back seat of a vehicle until they are:
options: 6 years old
9 years old
13 years old
16 years old
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: it states that all children should ride in the back seat of a vehicle until 13 years old.

q: A belt-positioning booster seat should generally be used until a child is about:
options: 100 cm (about 2-4 years)
145 cm (about 4-8 years)
170 cm (about 12 years)
Booster seats are never needed in the UAE
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: children should use belt-positioning booster seats until they are about 145cm (4'9") tall, roughly 4 to 8 years old.

q: According to the RTA handbook, pregnant women in a vehicle should:
options: Not wear a seatbelt to protect the baby
Wear a seatbelt, to protect both themselves and their unborn child
Only wear the lap portion of the belt
Sit in the back seat unbelted
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: pregnant women need to also use a seat belt to keep themselves and their unborn child safe.

q: In Dubai's paid parking system, 'Code A' side-road parking areas allow a maximum short stay of:
options: 1 hour
4 hours
12 hours
24 hours
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: Code A refers to side-road parking areas with a short-stay maximum of 4 hours, while Code B parking yards allow up to 24 hours.

q: In Dubai's paid parking system, a 'Code B' parking yard allows a long-stay of up to:
options: 4 hours
8 hours
24 hours
48 hours
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: Code B refers to areas specifically created as a parking yard, allowing long stays of up to 24 hours.

q: Non-payment of parking fees or a lost paid-parking ticket in a multi-storey car park carries a fine of:
options: AED 100
AED 150
AED 200
AED 500
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook's parking violations table: non-payment of the parking fees or a lost ticket (in an MSCP) carries a fine of AED 150.

q: Exceeding the paid parking duration you have paid for carries a fine of:
options: AED 50
AED 100
AED 300
AED 600
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook's parking violations table: exceeding the paid parking duration carries a fine of AED 100.

q: Parking in a disabled parking bay without the appropriate permit carries a fine of:
options: AED 100
AED 200
AED 500
AED 1000
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook's parking violations table: parking on a disabled parking space without the appropriate permit carries a fine of AED 500, the highest of the listed parking violations.

q: A 'No Parking' sign means you must not park in the area even if:
options: It is after 10pm
You remain seated in the vehicle
You have hazard lights on
It is raining
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: for a 'No Parking' area, you must not park there, even if you are sitting in the vehicle.

q: A 'No Stopping' sign means:
options: You may stop briefly to drop off a passenger
You must not stop at the kerb for any reason
You may stop only during the day
You may stop if hazard lights are on
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: 'No Stopping' signs tell you that you must not stop at the curb for any reason, and you must obey them.

q: A sign marking a loading/unloading zone means that, outside a commercial vehicle actively loading or unloading within the shown times, you must:
options: Not park there during those times
Park there for free all day
Only park motorcycles there
Use it as a taxi rank
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: these areas are reserved for vehicles loading or unloading at specific times; unless you are driving a commercial vehicle doing so, you must not park there during those times.

q: You must not cross a single solid line on the road dividing traffic. This rule comes from which article of the UAE Federal Traffic Law's Executive By-Law?
options: Article 33
Article 36
Article 54
Article 58
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: Article 58 of the Executive By-Law states you must not cross a single solid line on the road which divides traffic.

q: Diagrammatic warning signs (showing lane layouts, such as lanes merging) are typically used:
options: Only in residential streets
On high-speed roads where a simple triangular sign wouldn't give enough detail
Only at pedestrian crossings
Instead of traffic lights
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: diagrammatic warning signs are used where the triangular advance warning sign does not allow enough room for a picture, usually on high-speed roads, for situations like an additional lane, regulated lane use, or lanes merging.

q: According to Article 1 of the Executive By-Law of UAE Federal Traffic Law No. 21 of 1995, every road user must:
options: Drive as fast as conditions allow
Follow signs, signals and police instructions and behave so as not to endanger or block others
Always take priority over other vehicles
Only follow the rules when a police officer is present
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook (Article 1): every road user must respect traffic regulations, follow signs, signals and police instructions, and behave cautiously so as not to harm others, expose them to danger, or block their movement.

q: According to Article 36 of the Executive By-Law, when you are turning into a road, you must:
options: Sound your horn to warn pedestrians
Give way to pedestrians crossing the road you are turning into
Only give way if pedestrians are elderly or disabled
Proceed first if your indicator was on early
explanation: Verified in the RTA handbook: Article 36 requires drivers to always give way to pedestrians who are crossing the road they are turning into.

q: A motorcyclist should always buy a new helmet rather than a second-hand one mainly because a second-hand helmet:
options: Is always the wrong size
May have hidden damage that is not visible but weakens its protection
Is always an outdated design
Costs more to maintain
explanation: This is standard motorcycle-safety guidance (also used in UAE motorcycle rider training materials): a second-hand helmet may have sustained impact damage that isn't visible but that seriously reduces its ability to protect in a crash.

q: After you press the brake pedal on a heavy vehicle with air brakes, there is a delay before the brakes fully act. About how long is this delay?
options: No delay at all
Up to about one second
About 10 seconds
About one minute
explanation: Air takes time to travel through the system after the pedal is pressed — up to about a one-second delay — so heavy-vehicle drivers must start braking earlier than in a light vehicle (Truck and Bus Handbook).

q: On a long downhill, continuous heavy braking causes “brake fade” because:
options: The brake linings overheat and gradually lose their stopping power
The brake pedal physically locks in place
The tyres automatically deflate
The engine shuts off to protect itself
explanation: Continuous heavy braking on a long hill heats up the brake linings until they no longer slow the vehicle effectively — this is called brake fade (Truck and Bus Handbook).

q: To help prevent brake fade before starting down a long hill in a heavy vehicle, you should:
options: Shift into a lower gear before you start going down
Shift into neutral and coast down
Turn off the engine to save fuel
Apply the handbrake fully for the whole descent
explanation: Shifting into a lower gear before a long descent lets engine braking help slow the vehicle, so the brakes are used less and are less likely to overheat and fade (Truck and Bus Handbook).

q: Because a heavy vehicle takes longer to slow down and stop, a driver should look ahead on the road for about how many seconds' worth of travel?
options: 2-3 seconds
12-15 seconds
30-40 seconds
Less than 1 second
explanation: Heavy-vehicle drivers need to know what is on the road 12 to 15 seconds ahead, since large vehicles take longer to slow down, change lanes, or stop (Truck and Bus Handbook).

q: When a long heavy vehicle goes around a turn, the rear wheels usually follow a shorter, tighter path than the front wheels. This is called:
options: Cut-in
Aquaplaning
Brake fade
Double-clutching
explanation: This effect is called “cut-in”; the sharper the turn and the longer the vehicle, the greater the cut-in, so drivers must position their approach accordingly (Truck and Bus Handbook).

q: When reversing an articulated (trailer) heavy vehicle, the trailer:
options: Moves in exactly the same direction the steering wheel is turned
Moves contrary to (opposite of) the direction the steering wheel is turned
Cannot move at all while reversing
Straightens itself automatically without steering input
explanation: The trailer moves contrary to the direction of the steering when reversing, so drivers need special technique and practice, using all mirrors and correcting drift immediately (Truck and Bus Handbook).

q: If you are involved in a traffic accident in Dubai, the police must be notified within:
options: 1 hour
6 hours
24 hours
48 hours
explanation: The RTA Light Motor Vehicle Handbook states the police must be notified within 6 hours of a crash, and you must give a truthful account of what happened.

q: If the police accident report finds you were at fault, before your confiscated licence is returned, you generally need to:
options: Pay a personal fee directly to the officer
Take the accident form to your insurance company and get a letter confirming your claim, then present it to police
Wait exactly 90 days automatically with no other action
Sell your vehicle first
explanation: The at-fault driver's licence is taken at the scene; you must take the accident form to your insurance company, which gives you a letter you take back to the police station to get your licence returned (RTA Light Motor Vehicle Handbook).

q: In Dubai, after a minor crash where both vehicles are still driveable, drivers should:
options: Leave the vehicles exactly where they stopped, no matter what
Move the vehicles to the side of the road to avoid blocking traffic — leaving them can result in a fine
Push the vehicles into the nearest police station themselves
Swap number plates with the other driver
explanation: If a crash occurs where both vehicles can still be driven, the handbook says they should be moved to the side of the road to stop traffic build-up; drivers who fail to move them can be fined (RTA Light Motor Vehicle Handbook).

q: To renew your Dubai vehicle registration (Mulkiya) through an RTA Trusted Agent (such as a selected insurer), you must first:
options: Sell your current vehicle
Purchase vehicle insurance
Retake the practical driving test
Take a new eye test at an optician
explanation: Selected vehicle insurers act as RTA Trusted Agents: to renew your registration through them you must purchase vehicle insurance, and they can then register the vehicle for you (RTA Light Motor Vehicle Handbook).

q: Under UAE Federal Traffic Law (Article 12), if you witness a traffic accident, you must:
options: Drive away immediately to avoid being delayed
Give every possible assistance to the victims, especially the injured
Only take photographs and then leave the scene
Wait for a lawyer to arrive before doing anything
explanation: Article 12 of the Executive By-Law of UAE Federal Traffic Law No. 21 of 1995 requires all road users to give every possible assistance to accident victims, especially those who are injured (RTA Light Motor Vehicle Handbook).

q: Under UAE Federal Traffic Law (Article 10.7), you must not drive your vehicle when:
options: Tired, as you may become unable to control your car
The fuel tank is below half full
You are wearing sunglasses
You have passengers under 18
explanation: Article 10.7 of UAE Federal Traffic Law No. 21 of 1995 states you must not drive when tired, as you may become unable to control your car (RTA Light Motor Vehicle Handbook).

q: Which of the following is a warning sign that you should stop driving and rest?
options: Constant yawning and starting to drift across your lane
Feeling fully alert and focused on the road
Driving exactly at the posted speed limit
Checking your mirrors regularly
explanation: The RTA Light Motor Vehicle Handbook lists constant yawning, drifting across the lane, fuzzy eyesight, and not remembering the last few kilometres driven as signs that it is time to stop and rest.

q: The RTA Light Motor Vehicle Handbook notes that in one month in Dubai, how many people died due to careless and sleepy driving?
explanation: The handbook states: “In one month in Dubai alone, 13 people died due to careless and sleepy drivers,” used to underline the danger of driving while tired.

q: A red-ringed circular sign showing a horn symbol with a diagonal line through it means:
options: Sounding your horn is prohibited in this area
Horn use is mandatory in this area
This is a hospital ahead
No entry for vehicles with trailers
explanation: A red circular prohibitory sign with a horn and a diagonal strike-through bans sounding the vehicle horn — common near hospitals, mosques, and residential areas.

q: A blue circular sign showing a number followed by "km/h" with no red border generally means:
options: This is the maximum speed allowed
This is the minimum speed required, conditions permitting
This is a suggested speed only
This speed applies only to trucks
explanation: Blue circular signs are mandatory instructions; a blue circle with a speed figure (unlike the red-ringed maximum-speed sign) sets a minimum speed drivers must maintain where conditions allow, common on fast highway lanes.

q: A blue circular sign with a white arrow pointing to the right means:
options: Right turn is one option among several
You must turn right; going straight or left is not allowed at this point
Right lane is closed ahead
No right turn is allowed
explanation: Blue circular mandatory signs with a directional arrow require traffic to follow that exact direction — right only, with no option to continue straight or turn left at that point.

q: A yellow/red triangular warning sign showing a stylised traffic light means:
options: Traffic signals ahead — be ready to slow down and stop
All traffic signals in this area are switched off
This is a pedestrian crossing
Photo enforcement cameras are active
explanation: Triangular warning signs alert drivers to a hazard or feature ahead; a traffic-light symbol warns that a signal-controlled junction is coming up, so drivers should be prepared to slow down and stop.

q: A triangular warning sign showing a car with wavy skid marks means:
options: Car wash facility ahead
The road surface ahead may be slippery — reduce speed and increase following distance
Speed bumps ahead
Vehicle testing centre ahead
explanation: This warning sign indicates the road surface may be slippery, for example after rain, sand, or oil — drivers should slow down and keep a larger following distance.

q: A blue rectangular sign showing a fuel pump symbol tells a driver that:
options: Fuel is banned in this area
A fuel/petrol station is nearby or just ahead
Overtaking is prohibited near fuel stations
This is a truck-only route
explanation: Blue rectangular informatory signs give useful information rather than commands or warnings; a fuel-pump symbol simply shows a petrol station is nearby or ahead.

q: Among standard road signs, the inverted (downward-pointing) triangle shape is reserved exclusively for:
options: Speed limit signs
The GIVE WAY sign
Hospital signs
No entry signs
explanation: By international convention (which UAE signage follows), the downward-pointing "inverted" triangle shape is used only for the GIVE WAY sign — no other sign uses this shape, so its outline alone is recognisable even without reading the words.

q: On UAE road signs, the colour red is generally used to indicate:
options: Directions and general information
Prohibition, danger, or a mandatory stop
Temporary roadworks only
Motorway/highway routes only
explanation: Red is used internationally (and on UAE signs) for prohibition (circles with red rings/diagonal bars), danger (warning triangles' red border), and the STOP sign — a colour drivers should always read as "restriction or hazard."

q: On UAE road signs, a blue background or blue circle generally indicates:
options: A warning of danger ahead
A mandatory instruction or general travel information
A temporary condition such as roadworks
A prohibition
explanation: Blue is used for mandatory instruction signs (circles telling drivers what they must do) and for informatory/guide signs (rectangles giving directions or facilities) — never for danger warnings or prohibitions.

q: Among standard road sign shapes, the eight-sided (octagon) shape is reserved exclusively for:
options: The STOP sign
Speed limit signs
Parking signs
Roundabout warning signs
explanation: The octagon is a unique shape reserved only for the STOP sign, by international convention that UAE follows — so it is recognisable by outline alone, even if a driver cannot read the word "STOP" or is approaching from behind (mirrored shape).

q: A seatbelt's shoulder strap should be worn:
options: Under the arm, across the ribs
Behind the back
Across the shoulder and chest, not under the arm or behind the back
Loosely, so it can be removed quickly if needed
explanation: A seatbelt only protects properly when the shoulder strap crosses the shoulder and chest and the lap strap sits low across the hips; wearing it under the arm or behind the back can cause serious injury in a crash instead of preventing it.

q: For a young child using a car seat, which position in the vehicle is generally considered safest?
options: Front passenger seat, facing forward
Rear seat
Front passenger seat, with the airbag switched off
It does not matter which seat is used
explanation: The rear seat is generally the safest place for a child restraint, away from the front airbags and the direct impact zone in a frontal collision.

q: On a hot day, leaving a child alone and unattended inside a parked vehicle, even for a short time, is:
options: Safe if the windows are slightly open
Dangerous — vehicle interior temperatures can rise very quickly and become life-threatening
Only a concern if the trip will be longer than one hour
Only a concern in vehicles without air conditioning
explanation: A parked vehicle's interior can heat up rapidly in the sun, even with windows cracked, and can become dangerous for a child within a short time — a child should never be left alone in a parked vehicle.

q: A booster seat is used to raise a child so that:
options: They can see out of the window better
The adult seatbelt fits properly across their shoulder and hips instead of their neck and stomach
They take up less space in the back seat
The car seat is easier to remove
explanation: A booster seat raises a child so the vehicle's own seatbelt sits correctly across the shoulder and hip bones — without one, the belt can sit across the neck and stomach, which is dangerous in a crash.

q: If another driver flashes their headlights at you to signal you can go first, you should:
options: Always proceed immediately, since the other driver has given you right of way
Still check the situation yourself — a headlight flash is a courtesy signal, not a guarantee of safety, and you remain responsible for judging it is safe to proceed
Ignore it and never move
Flash your own headlights back before doing anything else
explanation: Right of way is determined by traffic rules, signs, and signals — not by another driver's headlight flash. It can be a helpful courtesy, but you must still confirm it is actually safe before proceeding, since the signalling driver may not have seen a hazard.

q: You approach a junction where the traffic lights are completely dark (a power failure) and no police officer is directing traffic. You should:
options: Proceed at normal speed, since the lack of a red light means you have priority
Treat the junction with the same caution as an uncontrolled intersection — slow down, look carefully, and give way as needed before proceeding
Stop and wait indefinitely until the lights come back on
Sound your horn continuously while crossing
explanation: With no working signal and no officer directing traffic, a junction should be treated with the caution of an uncontrolled intersection: slow down, check all directions, and be prepared to give way, since no light is actively controlling right of way. (Flagged for verification of the exact UAE procedural rule, though the underlying caution is universal defensive-driving practice.)

q: In the UAE, right of way at an intersection with no traffic signals is decided mainly by:
options: Always giving way to the vehicle approaching from your right, in every case
Signs, road markings, and which road is the major/minor road — not an automatic "vehicle on the right" rule
Whichever vehicle is travelling faster
Whichever vehicle arrives first, regardless of signs
explanation: Unlike some countries' blanket "yield to the right" convention, right of way in the UAE is set by the actual signs, road markings, and road hierarchy at that junction (e.g. a GIVE WAY or STOP sign on the minor road) rather than a fixed left/right rule — always follow what the signs and markings actually say. (Flagged for verification against the exact statutory wording, since this is a common source of confusion between different countries' conventions.)

q: When two lanes merge into one because of a lane closure ahead (for example, roadworks), the safer technique is generally to:
options: Merge early and as soon as possible, regardless of the queue in the continuing lane
Use both lanes up to the merge point and take turns merging one vehicle at a time ("zip merging"), rather than everyone crowding into one lane early
Speed up in the closing lane to get ahead of as many vehicles as possible
Stop completely in the closing lane and wait for a gap
explanation: Taking turns merging one-for-one right at the point where a lane actually ends (rather than everyone squeezing into the continuing lane far in advance) uses the road's full capacity and reduces sudden braking and long queues — but it still requires courtesy and should never involve racing another vehicle to the merge point.

q: A vehicle's total stopping distance is the reaction distance (before the brakes are applied) plus the braking distance. As speed increases, this total stopping distance:
options: Stays roughly the same regardless of speed
Increases, and increases more sharply than speed itself (not just in direct proportion)
Decreases, because faster vehicles have better brakes
Only increases on wet roads
explanation: Reaction distance increases in direct proportion to speed, but braking distance increases with the square of speed — so doubling your speed more than doubles your overall stopping distance, which is why speeding is especially dangerous.

q: If you double your vehicle's speed, the distance needed to brake to a stop:
options: Stays about the same
Roughly doubles
Roughly quadruples (increases about four times), not just doubles
Roughly halves
explanation: Braking distance is related to the square of speed, so doubling your speed roughly quadruples the distance needed to stop — a key reason why even a small increase in speed can make a crash far more severe.

q: Driving while extremely fatigued mainly affects a driver because it:
options: Has no measurable effect on driving ability
Slows reaction time and impairs judgement, in a similar way to being under the influence of alcohol
Only affects a driver's comfort, not their ability to control the vehicle
Improves concentration by keeping the driver alert to discomfort
explanation: Severe fatigue slows reaction time and impairs judgement and attention in ways that resemble alcohol impairment, even though no alcohol is involved — which is why "drowsy driving" is treated as seriously as drink-driving in road safety guidance.

q: Before opening a car door after parking, a driver or passenger should:
options: Open it quickly to save time
Check mirrors and look for approaching traffic, cyclists, or pedestrians before opening the door
Only worry about this if parked in a garage
Assume it is always safe if the engine is switched off
explanation: Opening a door without checking can cause a collision with a passing vehicle, cyclist, or pedestrian — always look before opening, especially on the side facing traffic.

q: A motorcyclist's protective gear should generally include:
options: A helmet only; other gear is unnecessary
A full set of protective gear — helmet, jacket, gloves, and suitable footwear — since a crash can injure any part of the body
Sunglasses only, for glare protection
Gear is only needed for long trips, not short ones
explanation: A motorcyclist has far less physical protection than a car occupant, so a full set of protective gear (helmet, jacket, gloves, sturdy footwear) — not just a helmet — reduces the risk of injury to the whole body in a fall or crash.

q: A yellow/red triangular warning sign showing a person digging with a shovel means:
options: A pedestrian crossing is ahead
Roadworks are ahead on the road
A construction site entrance is nearby
Parking is reserved for workers
explanation: The 'roadworks ahead' warning sign uses the standard triangle shape with a silhouette of a person digging; it tells drivers to slow down and watch for workers, machinery, and possible lane changes ahead.

q: A blue rectangular sign showing a single bold white arrow pointing straight up, placed at a street entrance, indicates:
options: This is a one-way street; traffic may only travel in the arrow's direction
Two-way traffic is permitted on this street
This street is closed to all traffic
This is a pedestrian-only street
explanation: A one-way sign (a blue rectangle with a single directional arrow) placed at a street entrance means all traffic on that street must travel only in the direction the arrow shows.

q: A blue circular sign showing the black silhouette of a walking adult and child means:
options: Drivers must stop for any pedestrian nearby
A school is located on this street
This area is reserved for pedestrians only; motor vehicles must not enter
Pedestrians must use the crossing ahead
explanation: A blue circle (the mandatory-sign colour/shape) with a pedestrian silhouette marks a pedestrian-only zone: it instructs that only foot traffic is permitted there and motor vehicles must not enter.

q: A red-ringed circular sign showing a shape like a vehicle passing under a bar, with a number followed by 'm', warns that:
options: The road ahead has a minimum speed of that many metres per second
Vehicles taller than the height shown must not pass (a height/clearance restriction)
Parking is limited to that many minutes
The road narrows to that width ahead
explanation: A red-ringed circular sign with a vehicle-under-a-bar symbol and a number in metres is a height/clearance restriction: any vehicle taller than the stated height must not attempt to pass (common before low bridges or tunnels).

q: A red-ringed circular sign showing a truck silhouette with a number followed by 't' warns that:
options: Vehicles heavier than the stated total weight are not permitted
Only trucks are permitted on this road
Trucks must maintain that many metres of following distance
The road can support that many trucks at once
explanation: A weight-limit sign shows the maximum gross vehicle weight (in tonnes) allowed on that road, bridge, or route; any vehicle heavier than the stated limit must not use it.

q: A yellow/red triangular warning sign showing a bicycle symbol placed before a junction warns drivers that:
options: Bicycles are prohibited beyond this point
There is a bicycle repair shop ahead
A cycle race is in progress
Cyclists are likely to be crossing or joining the road ahead, so extra caution is needed
explanation: This warning triangle alerts drivers to an upcoming point where cyclists commonly cross or merge into traffic, so drivers should slow down, check mirrors and blind spots, and be ready to give way.

q: A red-ringed circular sign showing a bicycle symbol with a diagonal red line through it means:
options: Bicycles have priority on this road
Cyclists must dismount and walk
Cycling is prohibited on this stretch of road
Cyclists must ring a bell before proceeding
explanation: A red circle with a diagonal bar through a symbol is the standard prohibitory format; over a bicycle symbol it means cycling is not permitted on that stretch of road.

q: A small blue rectangular sign mounted above a specific lane, showing only a left-turn arrow, means:
options: Any lane may turn left from this point
Traffic in that specific lane must turn left; it cannot go straight or right
That lane is closed ahead
Left turns are prohibited from that lane
explanation: A mandatory direction sign placed above one lane applies only to that lane: drivers already in it must follow the shown arrow (here, turn left) and cannot use it to go straight or turn right.

q: A red-ringed circular sign showing a truck silhouette with a diagonal red line through it means:
options: Trucks/heavy goods vehicles are not permitted on this road
Only trucks may use this road
Trucks must stop and pay a toll ahead
Trucks must reduce speed on this road
explanation: A vehicle silhouette inside a red circle with a diagonal bar is a prohibition specific to that vehicle type; showing a truck means trucks and heavy goods vehicles are banned from that road or lane.

q: When a circular prohibitory sign shows a number (such as a weight or height limit), that number represents:
options: A recommended value drivers may exceed if traffic allows
The maximum permitted value; exceeding it is not allowed
The average value most vehicles use
The minimum value required to use that road
explanation: On prohibitory signs (red-ringed circles), a numeric value is always a legal maximum, not a suggestion or an average -- vehicles or speeds exceeding that number are not permitted to use the road.

q: A yellow/red triangular warning sign showing a truck tilted downward on an incline warns drivers of:
options: A speed bump ahead
A road that is closed to trucks
